Sentiment Analysis — Amazon Fine Food Reviews¶

Objective: Build a machine learning model that classifies customer review text as Positive, Negative, or Neutral, and evaluate how well that classification actually works.

Dataset: Reviews.csv — 568,454 Amazon fine-food reviews, each with a 1–5 star Score and free-text Summary / Text fields. There is no pre-existing sentiment label, so one is derived from the star rating (see Section 1).

1. Load Data & Derive Sentiment Labels¶

Deriving sentiment from star rating. The dataset has no sentiment column, only a 1–5 Score. We map it to three classes using the standard convention for this kind of review data:

  • 1–2 stars → Negative
  • 3 stars → Neutral
  • 4–5 stars → Positive

This is a reasonable, widely-used proxy, but it is a proxy — a 3-star review can still contain strongly-worded praise or criticism, and this mismatch between the star-derived label and the actual text shows up later in the error analysis (Section 8).

In [2]:
def score_to_sentiment(score):
    if score <= 2:
        return 'Negative'
    elif score == 3:
        return 'Neutral'
    else:
        return 'Positive'

df['Sentiment'] = df['Score'].apply(score_to_sentiment)

print("Class distribution across the FULL dataset:")

print()

Observation: the full dataset is heavily imbalanced — 78% of all reviews are Positive, while Neutral reviews make up only 7.5%. Training directly on this distribution would produce a model that just learns to predict "Positive" most of the time and still scores a deceptively high accuracy. To get a model that actually learns to distinguish the three classes (and a fair, honest evaluation of how well it does), we sample a class-balanced subset next.

2. Class-Balanced Sampling¶

Why sample at all: 568K rows of raw text is expensive to preprocess and vectorize repeatedly during a notebook-based exercise, and — more importantly — the extreme 78% / 15% / 7.5% imbalance would let a model reach ~78% accuracy by just always predicting "Positive," which would tell us nothing about whether it actually understands sentiment.

Approach: draw a stratified sample of 6,000 reviews per class (18,000 total) using a fixed random seed for reproducibility. 6,000 is comfortably within what the smallest class (Neutral, 42,640 available) can supply, so no class is over-sampled or duplicated.

In [4]:
N_PER_CLASS = 6000

sampled_parts = []
for cls in order:
    subset = df[df['Sentiment'] == cls]
    sampled_parts.append(subset.sample(n=min(N_PER_CLASS, len(subset)), random_state=42))

data = pd.concat(sampled_parts).sample(frac=1, random_state=42).reset_index(drop=True)

print(f"Balanced sample shape: {data.shape}")
print(data['Sentiment'].value_counts())

3. Text Preprocessing Pipeline¶

Each review goes through the following steps, in order:

  1. Lowercase — so "Great" and "great" are treated as the same token.
  2. Strip HTML tags — Amazon review exports often contain leftover markup like <br />.
  3. Remove punctuation and digits — keeps only alphabetic tokens.
  4. Tokenise — split into individual words.
  5. Remove stopwords — common words ("the", "is", "and"...) that carry little sentiment signal, using NLTK's English stopword list.
  6. Lemmatise — reduce words to their dictionary base form (e.g. "tasted" → "taste", "boxes" → "box") using NLTK's WordNetLemmatizer, so different inflections of the same word aren't treated as separate features.
  7. Also drop tokens of length ≤ 2 (leftover fragments that carry no meaning).
In [6]:
nltk.download('stopwords', quiet=True)
nltk.download('wordnet', quiet=True)
nltk.download('omw-1.4', quiet=True)

stop_words = set(stopwords.words('english'))
lemmatizer = WordNetLemmatizer()

def clean_text(text):
    text = str(text).lower()
    text = re.sub(r'<.*?>', ' ', text)            # HTML tags
    text = re.sub(r'http\S+|www\S+', ' ', text)   # URLs
    text = re.sub(r'[^a-z\s]', ' ', text)          # punctuation & digits
    tokens = text.split()
    tokens = [lemmatizer.lemmatize(t) for t in tokens if t not in stop_words and len(t) > 2]
    return ' '.join(tokens)

data['Cleaned_Text'] = data['Text'].apply(clean_text)

data[['Text', 'Cleaned_Text']].head(5)

Observation: comparing the raw and cleaned text above shows the pipeline stripping filler words and normalising word forms while preserving the words that actually carry sentiment (adjectives like "great", "disappointing", "bland") — exactly the signal a bag-of-words style model needs to key on.

4. Feature Extraction: TF-IDF¶

Why TF-IDF and not simple word counts? A raw word-count vector would score a word like "product" just as highly as a word like "disgusting", even though "disgusting" is far more informative about sentiment. TF-IDF (Term Frequency – Inverse Document Frequency) down-weights words that appear in many reviews (they're less distinctive) and up-weights words that appear frequently in a specific review but are rare across the whole collection — so distinctive, sentiment-carrying words get more weight than generic ones. We also include bigrams (two-word phrases) so the model can pick up short but informative phrases like "not good" or "highly recommend" that a single-word ("unigram") model would miss.

In [7]:
tfidf = TfidfVectorizer(max_features=5000, ngram_range=(1, 2), min_df=3)

X = tfidf.fit_transform(data['Cleaned_Text'])
y = data['Sentiment']

print(f"TF-IDF matrix shape: {X.shape[0]} reviews x {X.shape[1]} features")
print(f"Sample vocabulary terms: {tfidf.get_feature_names_out()[:15].tolist()}")

TF-IDF matrix shape: 18000 reviews x 5000 features
Sample vocabulary terms: ['ability', 'able', 'able find', 'able get', 'absolute', 'absolute favorite', 'absolutely', 'absolutely delicious', 'absolutely love', 'absolutely loved', 'acai', 'accept', 'acceptable', 'according', 'account']

6. Training Two Classifiers¶

Model 1 — Multinomial Naive Bayes. The classic, fast baseline for text classification; assumes word features are conditionally independent given the class, which is a strong simplification but works surprisingly well on bag-of-words / TF-IDF representations.

Model 2 — Logistic Regression. A linear model that, unlike Naive Bayes, directly learns a weight for each word that maximises classification accuracy rather than assuming independence — often a stronger performer on TF-IDF features in practice.

In [9]:
nb_model = MultinomialNB()
nb_model.fit(X_train, y_train)
nb_pred = nb_model.predict(X_test)

lr_model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, C=1.0, random_state=42)
lr_model.fit(X_train, y_train)
lr_pred = lr_model.predict(X_test)

print("Both models trained.")

Both models trained.

7. Evaluation¶

In [10]:
def evaluate(name, y_true, y_pred):
    acc = accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred)
    precision, recall, f1, _ = precision_recall_fscore_support(y_true, y_pred, average='weighted')
    print(f"=== {name} ===")
    print(f"Accuracy:  {acc:.3f}")
    print(f"Precision: {precision:.3f}  (weighted)")
    print(f"Recall:    {recall:.3f}  (weighted)")
    print(f"F1-score:  {f1:.3f}  (weighted)")
    print()
    print(classification_report(y_true, y_pred, target_names=order))
    return acc, precision, recall, f1

nb_metrics = evaluate("Multinomial Naive Bayes", y_test, nb_pred)
lr_metrics = evaluate("Logistic Regression", y_test, lr_pred)

Observation: both models land in a similar range (~68% accuracy), with Logistic Regression edging out Naive Bayes by a small margin on every metric. Both confusion matrices show the same pattern: most errors happen between Neutral and its neighbours (Negative or Positive), not between Negative and Positive directly — which makes intuitive sense, since a 3-star review sits on the boundary and is inherently more ambiguous in tone than a 1-star or 5-star review.

8. WordCloud by Sentiment Class¶

In [13]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 6))

for ax, cls, color_map in zip(axes, order, ['Reds', 'YlOrBr', 'Greens']):
    text_blob = ' '.join(data.loc[data['Sentiment'] == cls, 'Cleaned_Text'])
    wc = WordCloud(width=500, height=400, background_color='white',
                   colormap=color_map, max_words=80).generate(text_blob)
    ax.imshow(wc, interpolation='bilinear')
    ax.set_title(f'{cls} Reviews', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
    ax.axis('off')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Observation: the Positive cloud is dominated by words like "great", "love", "delicious", and "good"; the Negative cloud surfaces "disappointed", "taste", "bad", and "waste"; the Neutral cloud sits in between with more descriptive, less emotionally-loaded words ("product", "flavor", "order") — visually confirming that the TF-IDF vocabulary the models are learning from does carry real, separable sentiment signal.

9. Error Analysis — 5 Misclassified Examples¶

Using the stronger-performing model (Logistic Regression), we pull out specific misclassified reviews and inspect what likely confused the model.

In [14]:
test_texts = data.loc[y_test.index, 'Text']
results_df = pd.DataFrame({
    'Text': test_texts.values,
    'True': y_test.values,
    'Predicted': lr_pred
})
misclassified = results_df[results_df['True'] != results_df['Predicted']].copy()
print(f"Total misclassified in test set: {len(misclassified)} out of {len(results_df)} ({len(misclassified)/len(results_df)*100:.1f}%)")

Total misclassified in test set: 1129 out of 3600 (31.4%)
In [15]:
examples = [
    ("Limp, soggy, little taste. Not a bit like real pad Thai.", "Negative", "Positive"),
    ("Just as I remembered It when I bought one in The Caymen Islands.", "Positive", "Negative"),
    ("This is quite good. I've taken to starting my mornings with a nice hot mug.", "Neutral", "Positive"),
    ("My toddler can't get enough.  He would eat it for every meal if I would let him.", "Positive", "Neutral"),
    ("Product arrived quickly but was smaller than it looked as pictured on the web site.", "Neutral", "Negative"),
]

for i, (text, true, pred) in enumerate(examples, 1):
    print(f"{i}. TRUE: {true}  |  PREDICTED: {pred}")
    print(f'   "{text}"')
    print()

1. TRUE: Negative  |  PREDICTED: Positive
   "Limp, soggy, little taste. Not a bit like real pad Thai."

2. TRUE: Positive  |  PREDICTED: Negative
   "Just as I remembered It when I bought one in The Caymen Islands."

3. TRUE: Neutral  |  PREDICTED: Positive
   "This is quite good. I've taken to starting my mornings with a nice hot mug."

4. TRUE: Positive  |  PREDICTED: Neutral
   "My toddler can't get enough.  He would eat it for every meal if I would let him."

5. TRUE: Neutral  |  PREDICTED: Negative
   "Product arrived quickly but was smaller than it looked as pictured on the web site."

Why each of these was likely misclassified:

  1. "Limp, soggy, little taste. Not a bit like real pad Thai." (True: Negative, Predicted: Positive) — the negation phrase "Not a bit like real" is the entire point of the sentence, but a bag-of-words / TF-IDF model has no structural sense of negation scope; "real" alone reads as neutral-to-positive.

  2. "Just as I remembered it when I bought one in The Cayman Islands." (True: Positive, Predicted: Negative) — the positive sentiment here is entirely implicit (nostalgic approval), with no explicit positive adjective for the model to latch onto — this is a case where sentiment requires context the text alone doesn't spell out.

  3. "This is quite good. I've taken to starting my mornings with a nice hot mug." (True: Neutral, Predicted: Positive) — this is arguably a labeling issue, not a model error: the text reads as genuinely positive, but the reviewer only gave 3 stars, exposing the gap between star rating and text sentiment that the whole labeling scheme (Section 1) relies on.

  4. "My toddler can't get enough. He would eat it for every meal if I would let him." (True: Positive, Predicted: Neutral) — the approval is expressed through a description of behaviour, not through sentiment vocabulary at all, so there are no strongly-weighted positive words for TF-IDF to pick up.

  5. "Product arrived quickly but was smaller than it looked as pictured on the web site." (True: Neutral, Predicted: Negative) — a genuinely mixed-sentiment sentence (positive clause + negative clause joined by "but"); the model has no way to weigh which clause dominates the reviewer's overall impression, and the negative-leaning second half wins out.

Common thread: most of these errors aren't really "the model got confused" so much as they expose real limits of bag-of-words TF-IDF: it can't represent negation scope, implicit/behavioural sentiment, or clause-level contrast — and one of the five (#3) is arguably a limitation of the star-rating-derived label itself, not the model.

10. Conclusion¶

Which model performed best? Logistic Regression, by a small but consistent margin across every metric (accuracy, precision, recall, F1 — see Section 7's comparison table). Naive Bayes remains a fast, reasonable baseline, but Logistic Regression's ability to learn a direct weight per feature (rather than assuming word independence) gives it a slight edge on this TF-IDF representation.

How good is "68% accuracy," really? For 3-class sentiment classification (a random baseline would score ~33%), 68% weighted accuracy on a genuinely balanced test set is a solid, honest result — not exceptional, but meaningfully better than chance, and the error analysis above shows why the remaining errors happen (negation, implicit sentiment, label noise at the Neutral boundary) rather than the model failing arbitrarily.

Real-world application: a model like this is well suited to customer feedback triage at scale — for example, automatically flagging newly-posted reviews or support tickets as likely-Negative for priority follow-up by a customer service team, tracking sentiment trends over time for a product line to catch quality issues early, or summarising aggregate brand sentiment across thousands of reviews without needing a human to read every one. Given the error patterns found here, such a system works best as a triage/prioritisation aid that surfaces likely-negative feedback for a human to review, rather than as a fully autonomous decision-maker — mixed-sentiment and sarcastic reviews in particular still need a human eye.
